doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Why people call him: the Lionel Hampton date
summary: Rowe asks why so many artists hired him; Parker describes the Teo Macero-produced Lionel Hampton date with Grady Tate, Anthony Jackson, Joe Beck and Bobby Scott, then starts on Woodstock.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Well I was — I picked out four names and I was going to print out your discography but I didn’t have enough paper. So I picked four names: Lionel Hampton to Michael Bolton to Stuff to the Paul Butterfield Band.
So here’s a question, you’re going to have to set aside your modesty I think. Why have you played and recorded with so many people? Why do they choose Christopher Parker?
Yeah, you were way down the line, I know.

In each case it’s kind of different. Let’s see, Lionel Hampton was a date that Teo Macero produced and I had worked with Teo Macero on a Gato Barbieri record and he didn’t scare me. He was always kind of tempestuous you know, he had a temper and his face would get red and he would yell — I saw him yell at people you know who missed an eighth note in the second bar or something. But I wasn’t fazed by him on that — that’s the only thing I can think of, and I got a call for this Lionel Hampton date and I was thrilled, because Lionel Hampton’s records were things that I listened to as a kid and played along with and I always loved “Flyin’ Home” and “Gin for Christmas” and “Ring Dem Bells” and I saw him live a bunch of times, different concerts and theaters and stuff, and I was always knocked out by him. So this date I think Grady Tate is on one side and I’m on the other side. And my side is with a great bass player Anthony Jackson and we had worked together a lot. And Joe Beck on guitar and Bobby Scott on piano. So Lionel was great. And we got along and I of course told him how much I admired him and how much I had listened to him as a kid and everything and it was wonderful. Other than that I don’t know why I got the call. You mentioned Paul Butterfield — I was living in Woodstock and I initially moved there to join a rock band and then after the rock band we did one album and broke up.
